title: Mount an emergency-stop button in a panel hole with its tab in the notch and screw its locking ring on hand-tight
instruction: Mount the emergency-stop button in the panel hole with its tab in the notch, then screw its locking ring on from behind until it is hand-tight, and let go.
context: Machine control panels carry 22 mm push buttons, pilot lights, selector switches and emergency stops, all mounted one way: the operator goes into a keyed hole from the front and a locking ring is screwed onto its barrel from behind. One hand holds the operator, tab in the notch; the other screws the ring home and tightens it. An earlier review of this idea called it "regular work for electricians and team assemblers"; it falls under core O*NET tasks of electricians (47-2111.00) and of electrical and electromechanical equipment assemblers (51-2022.00, 51-2023.00). Counting only nonresidential and plant work, not the full occupations, BLS data (OEWS May 2025, QCEW 2025) give an estimated 371,600 electricians at nonresidential electrical contractors, 172,100 electricians employed outside building-equipment contractors, home builders and staffing agencies, and 89,900 assemblers in control-gear, machinery and instrument plants: about 633,600. No survey counts the operation itself (README).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y left; heights over the bench. A plate of 2 mm cold-rolled steel, 11 cm wide and 23 cm tall, its cut-out punched to the catalogue's size with a keyed knockout punch for 22 mm devices, stands upright between two posts screwed to the bench, on the midline, side-on to the arms: its front faces the right arm, its back the left. Its cut-out, 22.3 mm across with a 3.2 mm anti-rotation notch at the top, has its centre at x 25, y 0, 16 cm over the bench. An emergency-stop operator (IDEC HW1B-V4: 40 mm red mushroom head, threaded barrel M22 x 1 mm with a 0.5 mm gasket, contact block removed) stands head up on its stem's end at (30, -28) within 5 mm, with its locking ring (IDEC HW9Z-LN, 28.4 mm across, 5 mm high) two turns on the end of its thread, as supplied. By seed the operator is turned about its upright axis: its tab points 30, 120, 345 or 300 degrees from x. Both arms start in their ready pose; nothing is held.
scoring: Only the state at the end of the trial counts. 0: the button or the ring has fallen 2 cm or more under the bench top, or none of the levels below. 0.25: the button is in the hole with its tab in the notch and its gasket within 1 mm of the panel's front (seen from the back; a 1 mm feeler does not go under the bezel). 0.5: and the ring is at least one turn on the barrel behind the panel (it does not come off within a turn). 0.75: and the ring bears on the panel's back. 1.0: and the ring is hand-tight, 0.68 N m or more (a spring scale pulling the maker's ring wrench square to its handle at a mark r from the ring's axis does not turn it on below 0.68 N m / r), the button clamped (pulled out with 10 N on a spring scale, a 0.2 mm feeler does not go under the bezel), both grippers 3 cm or more from button and ring, everything at rest. A trial ends when the score has been 1.0 for one second.
reset_notes: Unscrew the ring, take the operator out of the panel, screw the ring two turns onto the end of its barrel and stand the operator head up on its stem's end on its mark at (30, -28), its tab turned as the seed gives (four marks on the bench), within 5 degrees. The gasket stays on the barrel, the contact block stays off, the panel stays in its frame. The start is checked from above against the start picture. A reset takes about one minute. The parts are reused; a ring or barrel with a damaged thread is replaced.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX; round parts are polygons. The thread is a mechanism, not flank contact: the ring runs 1 mm a turn on a hidden carrier and is taken on only in line (1 mm, 5 degrees) and turned on. The barrel is drawn into the bore within 1 mm and 5 degrees of its line, the tab within 5 degrees of the notch (real play 0.15 mm; the lead-in and the hand's give stand in for the rest). Tightening is a spring past first contact; the ring has 50 g of inertia (real 2 g).
